stories.headline: Denver man arrested at airport in fatal stabbing of his mother
stories.summary:
A Denver man has been arrested and charged with first-degree murder in the fatal stabbing of his mother. Denver police were called around 1:35 p.m. Sunday to the 4300 block of North Shoshone Street on a report of an unresponsive person and found a woman with stab wounds who was pronounced dead at the scene. Investigators identified her son, Johnathan Paul Villa, 42, as the suspect and believe the stabbing occurred several days earlier.

According to the arrest affidavit, the victim had asked police on Friday to conduct a welfare check on Villa. She told officers she felt unsafe, that he had previously assaulted her, and that she wanted him taken to a hospital for evaluation. Police said they did not have grounds to arrest or detain him. Neighbors later reported hearing screams around 10:15 p.m. Friday, and another resident of the home said he saw two knives with a red substance in the backyard.

Police said Villa had a history of violence, including a 2023 arrest for assault by strangulation involving his mother. Her phone, missing from the home, was pinged at Denver International Airport, where Villa was found in the outside plaza area and arrested. He was booked into the Denver jail Monday and is being held without bond.

stories.headline: Denver-based elder care provider InnovAge to pay $36 million settlement
stories.summary:
InnovAge, a Denver-based elder care organization, will pay $36 million to settle allegations that it failed to provide necessary services to people in its care. The Colorado Attorney General's Office and the U.S. Attorney's Office in Denver reached the agreement.

Authorities alleged the company did not give clients the care required in order to receive Medicaid payments. InnovAge operates programs serving seniors who need a nursing-home level of care but live in the community.

The settlement resolves the allegations brought by state and federal officials and carries significance for older Coloradans and families who rely on such programs.

stories.headline: Denver-area Realtor numbers drop amid prolonged housing slump
stories.summary:
The number of registered Realtors in the Denver area has fallen significantly since the pandemic-era housing boom. The decline follows a market in which mortgage rates near 7% and fewer home sales have squeezed agents' business.

The drop reflects a prolonged slump that has reduced transaction volume across the metro area. Many agents who entered the profession during the hot market have apparently left as sales slowed.

The trend illustrates how higher borrowing costs continue to ripple through the region's real estate industry and the broader housing market.

stories.headline: Homebuilder challenges Denver affordable housing requirements in federal appeals court
stories.summary:
Denver-based redT Homes LLC, a builder specializing in entry-level homes in neighborhoods such as Berkeley and Sunnyside, argued before the 10th Circuit that Denver's Mandatory Affordable Housing Ordinance is unconstitutional. The Pacific Legal Foundation presented oral arguments on the company's behalf Monday.

The ordinance, in effect since 2022, requires builders to either set aside some homes at below-market prices or pay a linkage fee on each home to support affordable housing. The company argues this amounts to an uncompensated taking under the Fifth Amendment. CEO Nathan Adams said the costs are being passed on to buyers.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado dismissed the case at the city's request, ruling redT could only challenge the law as a per se physical taking. The city attorney's office has maintained the ordinance does not violate the Fifth Amendment, and did not respond to the Gazette's request for comment.

stories.headline: Colorado exit poll: Trump voter drop-off and anti-Trump sentiment shaped 2026 results
stories.summary:
An exit poll from the nonpartisan Colorado Polling Institute found that turnout, opposition to President Donald Trump and left-leaning younger voters drove this year's results. The poll surveyed 606 voters statewide from Oct. 30 to Nov. 5, with a margin of error of 3.98 percentage points.

Pollsters said a drop-off among voters who backed Trump in 2024 was a key factor. In El Paso County, about half of those polled had voted for Trump in 2024 and half for Harris, though Trump won the county by about 10 points. Nearly half of respondents said their congressional votes were meant to signal opposition to Trump, versus 18% who meant to signal support.

Three Republican members of Congress who aligned closely with Trump lost their reelection bids as districts swung 10 or more points toward Democrats. Rep. Jeff Hurd of Grand Junction, who split with the president on tariffs and healthcare subsidies, was the lone Republican survivor.

stories.headline: Polis pardons four turkeys in annual pre-Thanksgiving tradition
stories.summary:
Gov. Jared Polis pardoned four Colorado-raised turkeys on Tuesday, saving them from Thanksgiving dinner tables in the state's annual tradition.

The birds were named for beloved icons who died in 2026. In a release, Polis said the turkeys will live out their lives at Luvin Arms, an animal sanctuary.

He said their long and happy lives will demonstrate Colorado's gratitude for the women, who he said changed the state and world through joy, laughter, activism and a commitment to justice and equality.

stories.headline: Powerful winds and high fire danger forecast for Front Range and Denver metro
stories.summary:
A potentially damaging wind event is expected to develop overnight and continue into Wednesday morning, with gusts of 70 mph or more possible in parts of the Front Range. A High Wind Warning is in effect for the northern mountains and foothills from 11 p.m. Tuesday through 11 a.m. Wednesday, with gusts of 60 to 75 mph expected.

The Boulder-to-Golden corridor along Highway 93 could see gusts of 40 to 50 mph between 7 a.m. and noon, and areas along I-25 north of Fort Collins could see similar gusts. A Red Flag Warning is in effect from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. for the southern metro and parts of the Palmer Divide, and a Fire Weather Watch covers the Denver metro and areas north along I-25.

A storm from Nevada will bring 2 to 4 inches of snow to the Park Range. Thursday should be calmer, with highs in the mid to upper 50s, before another system arrives Thursday night into Friday. Cooler-than-normal temperatures are likely through much of next week.

stories.headline: Colorado parents push to guarantee daily recess for students
stories.summary:
A new Colorado chapter of Say Yes to Recess, a national grassroots nonprofit, is pushing to mandate daily recess for elementary and middle school students. The chapter formed earlier this year with nine mothers and its Facebook group now has hundreds of members.

The group seeks 45 minutes of daily recess for elementary students and 30 minutes for middle schoolers, and wants to bar teachers from taking it away as discipline. Members have held more than 80 meetings with lawmakers, school boards and administrators, and several spoke at the Nov. 5 Denver Public Schools board meeting. They hope a bill is sponsored for the 2028 legislative session.

Current state law requires 600 minutes of physical activity per month, which can include PE classes and field trips, so schools can meet it while still removing recess. A DPS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

stories.headline: Colorado Coalition for the Homeless employees rally for safer working conditions
stories.summary:
Employees at the Colorado Coalition for the Homeless and members of SEIU Local 105 held a rally outside the organization's offices in Denver on Tuesday afternoon. They called for safer work conditions.

More than 10,000 people experienced homelessness in the Denver metro area in 2025, underscoring the demand on service providers and their staff.

stories.headline: Parts of I-25 in Denver shut down overnight after police pursuit
stories.summary:
Police activity shut down parts of Interstate 25 in both directions in Denver overnight Tuesday, the Denver Police Department said.

Officers chased a felony menacing suspect onto the highway, which led to the closures.

stories.headline: Westminster police seek man on Onewheel who allegedly exposed himself at McKay Lake
stories.summary:
Westminster police are asking for help identifying a man who allegedly exposed himself to a woman at McKay Lake, a public lake, on Nov. 9.

The suspect is described as a white man with black hair who wore a black hoodie with a design and was riding a Onewheel. Police released photos of the suspect and the hoodie.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Metro Denver Crime Stoppers at 720-913-7867.

stories.headline: Avalanche face week without MacKinnon and Makar
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche enter the week of Nov. 16-22 without Nathan MacKinnon and Cale Makar, who both suffered lower-body injuries in the Nov. 12 overtime loss to the Ottawa Senators. Coach Jared Bednar said MacKinnon is expected to miss about a month and Makar about two weeks.

Colorado is coming off a 4-1 win over Montreal on Nov. 14 and remains well positioned in the Central Division. Forwards Martin Necas, Artturi Lehkonen and Gabriel Landeskog are expected to take on larger roles, with Lehkonen leading the team in goals.

The coaching staff will also need to redistribute minutes among the remaining defensemen while Makar recovers.

topStory.headline: Xi Greets Trump at Shenzhen Airport in Rare Gesture Ahead of First Three-Way Summit With Putin at APEC
topStory.summary:
Chinese leader Xi Jinping personally greeted President Donald Trump on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport on Wednesday, embracing him as he stepped off Air Force One. The gesture was unusual: Xi did not meet Trump at the airport during Trump's visit to Beijing in May, and NBC News reported it is believed to be the first time Xi has greeted any U.S. president on arrival in China. A crowd of performers in colorful costumes waved flags and flowers and chanted "warm welcome" in Mandarin as Xi stepped out of his car.

The greeting reciprocated Trump's decision in September to meet Xi at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington before a White House state visit, a rare move for a U.S. president that drew criticism from lawmakers of both parties. Earlier in the day Xi met Russian President Vladimir Putin, who had been received at the airport by a lower-ranking Chinese official. Xi described the Chinese-Russian relationship as "steadfast as a rock through wind and rain," and in remarks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum he pitched China as a defender of the globalized economy and criticized protectionism. After arriving, Trump shook hands with Putin at the summit, took part in the leaders' group photograph, and attended a welcome banquet and cultural gala.

The leaders of the United States, China and Russia are scheduled to hold joint talks on Thursday, which would be the first trilateral meeting of the three. NBC News described the agenda as including high-stakes discussions on nuclear disarmament. Trump will also meet Xi separately, their third encounter this year. Putin's foreign affairs adviser, Yuri Ushakov, told Russian state media that Putin and Trump would speak several times during the summit, including at the gala dinner, at the plenary session and after its conclusion, even though no formal bilateral meeting has been announced. Trump has said he would welcome a separate meeting with Putin if the opportunity arose.

On the sidelines, Trump met Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney at his hotel in Shenzhen, according to a White House official; Sheinbaum called her session with Trump and his team "very good." Trump arrived after a brief stop in the Philippines, where he touted a potential nuclear energy deal. In his banquet speech, Xi highlighted Shenzhen's transformation from a small fishing village into a "city of innovation" and said he hoped Thursday's Economic Leaders' meeting would produce "tangible results." Trump is the first sitting U.S. president to visit Shenzhen, China's leading technology hub.

The summit unfolds against several pressures. A fragile trade truce between the United States and China is set to expire in January, and the two countries remain at odds over access to raw materials, advanced chips and markets. The New York Times reported that the trip has been shadowed by the Nvidia scandal: chief executive Jensen Huang was forced to resign last week after revelations of an extramarital affair with a businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence determined was spying for China. Trump has said he will not raise the matter or other issues of Chinese interference in American affairs with Xi. The Times also noted that the Chinese leader is balancing his close partnership with Russia against a far larger economic relationship with the United States, a balance on display in his handling of the two arrivals.
